item.title: ITIL certifications: levels and pathways
item.description:
In short:

  1. An ITIL certification validates knowledge of a service management framework, not mastery of a tool.
  2. The ITIL 4 scheme rests on a single foundation, then on designations obtained by accumulating modules and a Master level based on experience.
  3. A version 5 of the framework is rolling out in phases, with a simplified qualification structure and a bridge module for ITIL 4 certificate holders.
  4. The widely repeated five-level model describes a withdrawn version of the framework.

Looking for information on ITIL certifications quickly runs into a problem: the best-ranked pages do not all describe the same scheme. Some list five successive levels, others speak of designations, others still announce a new version. This confusion is not harmless, as it leads candidates to aim for a title that is no longer awarded. Setting the scheme straight means separating what belongs to the current framework, to its ongoing evolution, and to withdrawn versions whose documentation keeps circulating.

item.title: Incident and problem management: stop confusing them
item.description:
In short:

  1. An incident is measured in time to restore, a problem in incidents avoided.
  2. A workaround closes an incident but never closes a problem.
  3. Grouping recurring incidents is the main entry signal for problem management.
  4. A known error is a problem with an identified cause and a documented workaround, ahead of the permanent fix.

Two practices, two clocks

An incident is an unplanned interruption to a service or a reduction in its quality. The associated practice pursues one objective: restore service as quickly as possible. Restart, fail over, reassign a licence, the means hardly matter, including when they fix nothing fundamental.

item.title: ITIL 4: the 7 guiding principles explained
item.description:
In short:

  1. ITIL 4, published in 2019, places seven guiding principles ahead of its 34 management practices.
  2. These principles are rules of conduct, not processes to execute: they exist to arbitrate, not to run.
  3. Three of them, start where you are, keep it simple and progress iteratively, are enough to frame most projects.
  4. The framework cannot certify an organisation: that certification falls under the ISO/IEC 20000 standard.

Why ITIL 4 starts with principles

Earlier ITIL versions mostly described processes. ITIL 4 reverses the order and sets out seven guiding principles, valid in any context, before going into practice detail. The intent is explicit: avoid the mechanical application of a procedure catalogue to an organisation whose actual maturity nobody has examined.

item.title: ESM vs ITSM: what actually changes
item.description:
In short:

  1. ITSM and ESM rest on the same objects: service catalogue, ticket, priority, turnaround commitment, knowledge base.
  2. The only structural difference is scope: IT for ITSM, every support function for ESM.
  3. Moving from one to the other is a governance project, not a technical one.
  4. Three technical capabilities gate the transition: multiple catalogues, multiple assignment queues, partitioned access rights.

Two acronyms, one mechanism

ITSM organises the services delivered by the IT department. ESM applies the same reasoning to every function delivering an internal service. The building blocks are identical: describe a service, open a channel to request it, assign the request to someone, commit to a deadline, measure.
